segments.text: Part 3. You will hear two business students, Jenna and Tyler, planning a group project on food waste in campus cafes. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.
That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers.

part.title: Planning a food waste project

turns.text: Okay, Tyler, we need to get our plan for the food waste project to Professor Haddad by Friday. Shall we start with why we picked the topic? She wants that in the introduction.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Sure. I mean, there were some good ideas on her list of suggested topics, like the one on coffee cup packaging, but we didn't go with any of those.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: No. It really came from you, didn't it? From your job.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yeah. When I was working shifts at a campus cafe last semester, I couldn't believe how much went in the trash at closing. Whole trays of muffins and sandwiches. That's what got me thinking about it.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Right. And it's not as if the data's easy to get, so we can't say we chose it because it was convenient.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Ha, no, definitely not.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Okay, next, which cafe. I know we talked about the student union one.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Well, it's the busiest, so it would have been ideal, but the manager there turned us down. Too busy, she said.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: What about the little place in the science building?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I looked into that, but it only sells coffee and a few snacks. There just wouldn't be enough waste to measure. So the library cafe is really our best option, and the manager there's already said yes.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Great, the library one it is. Now, how do we actually measure the waste? My first thought was just counting the items left unsold at the end of the day.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: That would be quicker, but it misses everything people leave on their plates. Half-eaten sandwiches, that kind of thing.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: True. And I don't think taking photos of the trays would give us real numbers either.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Exactly. So I think we should weigh it. Everything that's thrown away, unsold or not, goes on a scale.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Okay, weighing it is. That'll be messy, but fine.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: We also wanted a short survey for customers, right? About why they leave food.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Yeah, but I've got a worry about that. I don't think the length is a problem, we can keep it to five questions. And we'll probably get plenty of people filling it in if we offer a free cookie. My concern is that people won't be honest. Nobody wants to admit they throw away half their lunch.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Hmm, that's a fair point. Maybe we make it anonymous, so they feel more comfortable.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Good idea. And how long should we collect data for?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Ideally a whole month, to get a really clear picture. But with the deadline, that's not realistic.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Could we do just one week?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I think that's too short. If there's a special event or a quiz week, it would skew everything. Let's say two weeks. That gives us ten weekdays of results.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Two weeks, then. Fine. So let's map out the actual steps. The library cafe manager has agreed in principle, but she wants something in writing first.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Right. She asked us to email her a project outline, just a page explaining what we'll do and when. I'll send that tomorrow.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.say: Then we need equipment. I checked, and a decent scale online is about eighty dollars, which is a lot for us.
turns.text: Then we need equipment. I checked, and a decent scale online is about $80, which is a lot for us.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Way too much. Can't we get one somewhere on campus?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Actually, yes. The nutrition department has kitchen scales that students can borrow for a week at a time. I'll go and ask on Monday.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Perfect. And before we hand out the survey, we should test the questions on someone.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: I was going to try it on my roommates, but they'd just joke around. Why don't we test it on our tutorial group? They'll take it seriously.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Good. We can do that on Thursday.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Then the two weeks of data collection. Where are we recording the weights? I've got a notebook I could use.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Paper gets lost, though. Let's put everything straight into a shared spreadsheet, so we can both see it on our phones.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Sure. Once that's done, we compare what was thrown away with what the cafe ordered from its suppliers?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Actually, the manager said the ordering records are confidential. But she'll let us see the sales figures, so we can compare those with the waste.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Fine. And then I'd like to interview someone about why the waste happens. Not the manager again, though. We've already talked to her plenty.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: The kitchen staff would know more anyway. They're the ones who decide how much to bake each morning.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Great. So, interviews with them.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: And the last step is giving something back to the cafe. Professor Haddad suggested a short video, but I'm not sure.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That would take ages to edit. A written report would be more useful for the manager anyway. Something she can share with her boss.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Agreed. So, who does what?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: I'll handle the scales and the spreadsheet, since I'm on campus most mornings.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: And I'll do the outline and the survey, and set up the interviews, since I know a few of the staff. Then we write the report together.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Sounds like a plan.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.heard: Okay, Tyler, we need to get our plan for the food waste project to Professor Haddad by Friday. Shall we start with why we picked the topic? She wants that in the introduction.
Sure. I mean, there were some good ideas on her list of suggested topics, like the one on coffee cup packaging, but we didn't go with any of those.
No, it really came from you, didn't it? From your job.
Yeah, when I was working shifts at a campus café last semester, I couldn't believe how much went in the trash at closing. Whole trays of muffins and sandwiches. That's what got me thinking about it.
Right, and it's not as if the data's easy to get, so we can't say we chose it because it was convenient.
Ha, no, definitely not.
Okay, next: which café? I know we talked about the Student Union one.
Well, it's the busiest so it would have been ideal, but the manager there turned us down. Too busy, she said.
What about the little place in the science building?

I looked into that, but it only sells coffee and a few snacks; there just wouldn't be enough waste to measure. So the library café is really our best option, and the manager there has already said yes.
Great, the library one it is. Now, how do we actually measure the waste? My first thought was just counting the items left unsold at the end of the day.
That would be quicker, but it misses everything people leave on their plates. Half-eaten sandwiches, that kind of thing.
True, and I don't think taking photos of the trays would give us real numbers either.
Exactly, so I think we should weigh it. Everything that's thrown away, unsold or not, goes on a scale.
Okay, weighing it is. That'll be messy, but fine.
We also wanted a short survey for customers, right, about why they leave food?

Yeah, but I've got to worry about that. I don't think the length is a problem. We can keep it to five questions, and we'll probably get plenty of people filling it in if we offer a free cookie. My concern is that people won't be honest. Nobody wants to admit they throw away half their lunch.
Hmm, that's a fair point. Maybe we make it anonymous so they feel more comfortable.
Good idea. And how long should we collect data for?
Ideally a whole month to get a really clear picture, but with the deadline that's not realistic.
Could we do just one week?
I think that's too short. If there's a special event or a quiz week, it would skew everything. Let's say two weeks. That gives us ten weekdays of results.
Two weeks, then. Fine. So let's map out the actual steps. The library café manager has agreed in principle, but she wants something in writing first.
Right. She asked us to email her a project outline, just a page explaining what we'll do and when – I'll send that tomorrow.
Then we need equipment. I checked, and a decent scale online is about $80, which is a lot for us.
Way too much. Can't we get one somewhere on campus?
Actually, yes. The nutrition department has kitchen scales that students can borrow for a week at a time. I'll go and ask on Monday.
Perfect, and before we hand out the survey, we should test the questions on someone.
I was going to try it on my roommates, but they'd just joke around. Why don't we test it on our tutorial group? They'll take it seriously.
Good, we can do that on Thursday.
Then the two weeks of data collection. Where are we recording the weights? I've got a notebook I could use.
Paper gets lost though. Let's put everything straight into a shared spreadsheet so we can both see it on our phones.
Sure. Once that's done, we compare what was thrown away with what the cafe ordered from its suppliers?
Actually, the manager said the ordering records are confidential, but she'll let us see the sales figures so we can compare those with the waste.
Fine. And then I'd like to interview someone about why the waste happens. Not the manager again, though. We've already talked to her plenty.
The kitchen staff would know more anyway; they're the ones who decide how much to bake each morning.
Great, so interviews with them.
And the last step is giving something back to the cafe. Professor Haddad suggested a short video, but I'm not sure.
That would take ages to edit. A written report would be more useful for the manager anyway, something she can share with her boss.
Agreed. So, who does what?
I'll handle the scales and the spreadsheet, since I'm on campus most mornings.
And I'll do the outline and the survey and set up the interviews since I know a few of the staff, then we write the report together.
Sounds like a plan.
